questions.query: After all the checkout churn, which mechanism do the CI bootstrap steps actually run today — the agent's built-in sparse mode or the sparse-checkout plugin?
questions.gold_answer: The plugin. The #12371 conversion to the agent-native env var was reverted for the bootstraps on 2026-07-28: same-agent A/B put native at 55-108s vs the plugin's 10-13s (3.5-9x, plus two Configure Pipeline timeouts), because a --reference clone against the 17.9 GB EFS mirror with a blob filter repacks the mirror's objects locally. The control: the never-converted tests bootstrap stayed flat at 8-10s through the incident.
questions.notes: Two adoption notes ("SHIPPED & LIVE", "ACTIVATION COMPLETE 2026-07-27") are lexically stronger for adoption-status vocabulary and carry no supersede edge — the reverted-state note must win on recency, not linkage.

questions.query: The plugin-based checkouts are fast — is that because they read through the shared git mirror?
questions.gold_answer: No. The plugin's checkout hook replaces the agent's checkout phase and BUILDKITE_REPO_MIRROR is never set on this fleet, so its ${...:+--reference} expands to nothing — a real Lint infra job log shows every object line remote:-prefixed (652 KiB from GitHub, no --reference). The plugin wins via --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --no-checkout bounding the object set; the mirror contributes nothing to its path.
questions.notes: Polarity test: the note's own pre-correction body claimed the plugin used the mirror; the 2026-07-28 CORRECTION header inverts it. Serving the uncorrected mechanism section answers wrong.

questions.query: If we retire the shared NFS git mirror entirely, what would we actually lose — which steps read it, and what did the storage comparison measure?
questions.gold_answer: Only the default-checkout path reads the mirror; the 17 custom-checkout sites and the sparse-checkout plugin never touch it. Measured mirror state: 17.9 GB, 541 packs (drifting upward), no commit-graph, no multi-pack-index, gc guard NOT applied, EFS sustained read 12.9 MB/s. The A/B: a node-local copy beats EFS ~10x with pack count held constant (46/36s to 4/3s clone) and ~36x with commit-graph+MIDX added — storage medium dominates, pack topology is second-order, and the full repack never completed in 90 minutes.
questions.notes: Join of the mirror-usage census with the isolated benchmark; either alone answers half the question.

questions.notes: The task's "why this waits" gates the derivation doc's apparent readiness; both records needed for a correct plan.

Gotchas: the base profile must be tf, not auto-tf, and drive it through just — raw tofu picks up ambient SSO creds and fails backend init misleadingly.

questions.query: Can we provision the macOS build machines by hand — brew-install the toolchain and drop an agent hook on them?
questions.gold_answer: No — there are no self-hosted macOS machines. queue=macos is Buildkite-hosted (MACOS_ARM64_M4_6X28): a fresh ephemeral VM per job, agent hooks unsupported, no custom base image selectable. Bootstrap must live repo-side — the Darwin guard in .buildkite/hooks/pre-command installs pinned mise per job (PR #12436), and the pin is a correctness fix because the hosted image's brew node violates the repo engines range. Any runbook describing hand-provisioned mac operator machines is wrong.
questions.notes: Negation-shaped: the plausible hand-provisioning assumption is recorded as explicitly falsified, with the reason the wrong recon happened (no API query).

questions.query: Before we flip the default queue onto our own agent image, what evidence says the image can serve every hosted step, and where are the flip steps written down?
questions.gold_answer: The 2026-07-28 audit (5 parallel enumerator lanes + live-container verification of sha-bc36212a77) found zero tool gaps: busybox userland, the apk layer, pre-baked /opt/mise (node 22.23.1, just, jq), per-step mise install lists, and hosted injection (docker) cover every hosted-step executable; candidate gaps (sha256sum, awk strftime) were disproved in the running image. The flip itself is the Phase 4 runbook — registry push DONE (PR #12525, second -t fanning out to nscr.io/17hr3ju7pnpbc), then canary, then a gated default-queue cutover — updated mid-execution with live-confirmed identifiers.
questions.notes: Audit note + runbook join; the suggested canaries (build-docker-phase2, release-forgedb, tf-plan) live only in the audit.

questions.query: After an image refactor, job pods die trying to exec a literal 'start' binary. What contract did the image break?
questions.gold_answer: agent-stack-k8s sets Args:["start"] and never sets Command, so Kubernetes uses the image ENTRYPOINT and replaces CMD. The image must keep the official buildkite/agent shape — ENTRYPOINT [tini-static, --, buildkite-agent-entrypoint] + CMD [start], with the wrapper at /usr/local/bin/buildkite-agent-entrypoint (hardcoded by the checkout/command containers) and ssh-env-config.sh beside it. Baking the full agent command into ENTRYPOINT makes pods exec "start" as a binary and crash-loop. Probe: docker run --rm start --version.
questions.notes: Symptom-phrased single-record lookup for an invariant that looks refactorable.

questions.query: The compiler toolchain that ships its own libc keeps getting broken by agent image bumps. What's the standing rule, and why can't the pre-merge watch-list ever catch this class?
questions.gold_answer: Rule: the bundled Wolfi glibc/ld-linux tarballs under build/cxx must move in lockstep with every agent-image glibc bump — the generated wrappers force LD_LIBRARY_PATH but binaries still start under the image's PT_INTERP loader, and ld.so/libc skew aborts every clang/lld action (stack smashing, exit 134). Pre-merge detection is structurally impossible: the image is pushed manually, rolled out as a sha-pin bump under pkl/ which routes to test-infra (zero buck2), and PR jobs run on the currently deployed image — hence the post-rollout canary task. Durable fix direction: exec through the bundled ld-linux.
questions.notes: Prevention posture (rule note + canary-gap task); q003 covers the incident mechanism itself.

questions.query: mise can install buck2 straight from its registry — any reason not to just use that?
questions.gold_answer: Yes: the aqua registry hardcodes musl assets for every buck2 release after 2023-07-11, and musl-static buck2 deterministically crashes its spawned clang/lld children on the glibc CI agents (exit 134; gnu-works/musl-fails bisect against build 434). Pin -gnu via mise's http: backend with explicit per-platform URLs + sha256s and a tool_alias (PR #12420). When bumping the date pin, update all four URLs and re-run mise lock; if the lock ever shows the aqua backend again, delete the whole tools block and re-lock — tool-scoped lock patches URLs but never re-resolves the backend.
questions.notes: Operational trap with a non-obvious re-lock footgun; single record.

questions.query: A merged PR whose squashed body contained a dollar-brace expression broke a downstream build upload. Where does the second expansion come from?
questions.gold_answer: buildkite-agent pipeline upload expands env references once; the monorepo-diff plugin then uploads its GENERATED pipeline, and that second upload re-scans the already-substituted commit message as pipeline source. ${foo.bar} aborts the upload ("Expected an operator, got .") with the agent's stderr swallowed; $name is valid and silently expands empty. monorepo-diff v1.5.2 doubles $ in message/branch/commit but only when the trigger step leaves them unset — setting them explicitly to ${BUILDKITE_*} bypasses the guard (what PR #12630 removed). Never hand a commit message to a nested upload unescaped.
questions.notes: Mechanism lookup phrased from the incident, not the record title.

questions.query: We fixed the commit-message hazard in the tests bootstrap — do the release pipelines have the same hole?
questions.gold_answer: Yes, one: release.pkl evaluates release-phase2.pkl on the agent and pipes it into a nested pipeline upload, and phase-2 embeds BUILDKITE_MESSAGE directly — pkl knows nothing about the expansion pass, so a dev merge commit with $ syntax hits pass two. There is no plugin to hand escaping back to; the fix is doubling $ in pkl (test-sanddb.pkl documents the convention). Checked and NOT affected: test-scans (command watch configs, no build block) and build-docker-phase2 (no message field).
questions.notes: Same-failure-class sweep: mechanism note joined with the second-instance task, including the explicitly-cleared neighbors.

questions.query: One pipeline's steps changed behavior between two builds with no tree change in the window. How is that possible here, and which pipeline is exposed?
questions.gold_answer: vulcan is the only spec of the 15 with commands embedded server-side (upload_style: false — no Configure step), so its steps run whatever the server config says on WHATEVER commit triggers it. A server apply of a branch render (mise-era commands while dev lacked the root mise.toml) broke Linear-triggered runs with no tree change (build 221 passed aqua-era, build 222 failed mise-era). Rule: apply an embedded-command spec only when every branch it can run on supports the commands. As of 2026-07-27 all 14 server specs were converged to the merged mise tree and re-diff clean.
questions.notes: Incident note + convergence note; the second establishes the current state so the answer is not stale alarm.

questions.query: The infra-apply pipelines used to be able to go green while uploading zero steps. Is that hole closed?
questions.gold_answer: Closed. The guard was deliberately NOT synced from PR #12377 while the aqua-to-mise migration owned the live config (syncing from dev would have reverted the migration on the pipeline that applies infrastructure). After the migration merged, all three — pulumi-up, pulumi-preview, pulumi-drift-detection — were synced and verified live 2026-07-27: each configuration carries set -o pipefail before the pipe into the upload. The pulumi bootstraps come from pulumi-bootstrap.pkl, so the guard is maintained in both emitters.
questions.notes: Task whose head text reads like open work; the closure lives in the criterion trail. Title-weighted retrieval reports the hole as still open.

questions.query: Our design's traffic assumptions for busy tables — did the evidence from the two production deployments back them up?
questions.gold_answer: No. A2 claims 100k-10M rows and bursts of hundreds of writes/sec; the survey of both production repos measures two to three orders of magnitude less (sofi run_attempts ~3.3k/week, claims_submissions 259 rows, journeys 152 of a 5001 cap; aig ~26 in-flight cases, list capped at 200). The cost drivers A2 omits entirely: bytes per row (base64 xlsx in text columns, whole reports as single JSON blobs) and round-trips per user action (12 parallel reads on one case page; up to 6 for one index). A2 must be rewritten against measured volumes and everything sized against it re-derived.
questions.notes: Survey doc + refutation task join; the two repos are opposite extremes of one API, so citing either alone is half the evidence.

questions.query: Writers need the ids of rows they just inserted. Does our exec path hand anything back, and can callers mint ids themselves in SQL?
questions.gold_answer: Neither, today: ExecResponse carries op_id/seq/rows_affected and discards result rows, so RETURNING yields nothing; uuid() and random() are absent from the allowlist, so SQL-side minting is off too. Both surveyed customers depend on ids coming back (positional reconciliation of insert_many; re-reading a row for server-set created_at). Sand-layer out-of-band minting is a valid answer but must be a stated decision — and it must preserve UUIDv7's lexicographic-equals-chronological property, a load-bearing ORDER BY tie-break for sofi.
questions.notes: Decision-shaped gap the record exists to keep visible; single record.

questions.query: Every calendar/clock function is refused by the SQL surface. Is that over-broad, and can the authorizer hook just allowlist the safe ones?
questions.gold_answer: Over-broad: the exclusion exists for redo-replay determinism — right for now() and random(), wrong for pure functions like strftime('%Y-%m-%d', col) — and both customer repos bucket and sort on timestamps constantly. The hook alone cannot fix it: SQLite passes 'now' as an argument VALUE, so the authorizer sees only the function name and cannot tell date('now') from date(col). Narrowing needs prepare-time argument inspection or a documented client-side contract, not just an allowlist entry.
questions.notes: The sharp edge (argument-value 'now') is the load-bearing fact; vocabulary overlap with the record is low by construction.

questions.query: How do actor credentials work now — do we still have the server-side grant table and the policy push route?
questions.gold_answer: No — DQ34 replaced the policy-table machinery entirely. Two tiers: long-lived tenant tokens in the server TOML (schema push + admin audit; 403 on exec/query), and short-lived self-contained actor tokens sat1.<claims>.<mac> with claims {t, a, exp, tbl?}, MAC-keyed by SHA-256 of the tenant token — exactly the TokenDigest the server already stores — so any tenant-token holder mints offline; deliberately no mint endpoint, no server-side token storage; absent tbl means whole-db. policy_store, _sandsql_policy, TableGrant, push_policy and the planned policy route are deleted from the plan (Track A amended; the work was unstarted).
questions.notes: In-record supersession (the identity note's original grant-store half was overridden when DQ34 surfaced) plus the decision note; averaging the two designs is the failure.

questions.query: Do we still need the storage-format freeze settled before the replication phase proceeds?
questions.gold_answer: No — decided 2026-07-29 at Phase-3 planning: there is no format freeze before Phase 3. Nothing is deployed and no durable data must survive a binary upgrade, so the wipe-to-cross stance stands and the four items (redo V2 fingerprint registry + decode fallback, _sandsql_applied user_version migrations, E9 F1 per-frame admission attestation, SRF1 segment-identity headers) revert to ordinary backlog, picked up individually when a real upgrade path is needed.
questions.notes: Same in-record supersession shape as q025: the record's head still frames the freeze as one gate; the appended decision dissolves it. Polarity, not ids, is what scores.

questions.query: Table declarations, token minting, provisioning, the machine-readable SQL-surface spec — which component owns these, and when does it arrive?
questions.gold_answer: A new service crate, rust/crates/sandsql-api — one control plane for both Sand runtime targets (forge TS executor now, iris Go VM later) — owns the declaration registry (DQ32/DQ40 rollback/retirement semantics), sat1 mint mechanics verified against the single shared HMAC implementation, idempotent provisioning, and serving the SQL-surface spec (killing the sand side's hand-mirrored allowlist, their Q26). It ships as Phase 8, which blocks on Phase 7's additions push and the amended Track A tokens.
questions.notes: Decision note + phase task join; the ordering constraint (3 parallel 7, then 8) only exists across both.

questions.gold_answer: The corpus cannot answer. The rewrite has not run: the Part E task is open and GATED on an explicit recorded go, and both the v3.14 runbook and the operator sheet are pre-execution artifacts — the 72h soak exists only as a planned step. No observation exists.

questions.gold_answer: The corpus cannot answer. The conversion explicitly waits for a benchmark against the new node-local mirror, and the node-local rollout itself was reverted (#12571) after the LFS hang; only EFS-era regressions (native 3.5-4.3x slower) and mirror A/B numbers exist. No converted-site savings were ever measured.

questions.query: Does ccx still shell out to its old engine for any operation — symbol, deps, diff, anything?
questions.gold_answer: No — the tilth engine is gone as of v0.25.0 (2026-07-17), across four releases: v0.22 de-vendored ast-grep to a PATH dependency (0.44.0 floor), v0.23 native read/overview + ripgrep-only grep, v0.24 native outline-fallback/diff/history, v0.25 native symbol/deps with the internal/dispatch table (router, Backend interface, vendor, grok, and the diff regex grammar all deleted). The earlier "per-op peel-off, keep tilth for symbol/deps/diff" verdict is superseded — and the trigger was tilth's own stale index (a read --section off by 11 lines), not the grammar drift that verdict predicted.
questions.notes: Three-note arc (peel-off verdict -> rip-and-replace decision -> removal complete); the first note is the lexically richest for "tilth" and is wrong about the end state.

questions.query: My script passes a directory-scoping flag to ccx searches and now gets unknown-flag errors. What changed?
questions.gold_answer: File selection collapsed to one repeatable -g/--glob list in ripgrep's gitignore dialect (decided 2026-07-26 by a three-proposal design panel; all three judges converged on "keep the glob, delete the scope"). --scope is DELETED from all six commands that registered it — an unknown flag, not a deprecation. Migration: --scope D becomes -g D (a metachar-free glob naming a real directory normalizes to dir/**); the list is ordered, ! excludes, last match wins, and implementations must use StringArrayVarP so brace globs survive.
questions.notes: Deletion-not-deprecation temporal; stale fragment/AGENTS wording naming --scope is the magnet the corpus itself flags.

questions.query: ccx code grep sometimes takes tens of seconds. The story going around blames its gitignore handling on big dependency trees — is that right?
questions.gold_answer: No on both halves: --ignore-files is not a ccx flag at all (it comes from Claude Code's bundled-ugrep shell shim rewriting bare grep), and ignore handling usually pays for itself by pruning (module cache: 24.8s with vs 26.0s without; the repo itself 0.5s vs 4.3s). The real 2x is auto-regex escalation: a zero-match literal whose pattern compiles as a regex re-runs the FULL tree walk. Cost tracks tree size, not ignore-rule depth.
questions.notes: Circulating-diagnosis refutation; polarity scores, and the query deliberately repeats the wrong story.

questions.query: A post-mortem concluded the built-in Edit tool corrupts trailing whitespace and that caused the hook outage. Safe to build on that?
questions.gold_answer: No — falsified by live probes on 2026-07-15: Edit preserves trailing spaces byte-exact (end of new_string, interior, replace_all) and fails loudly on a whitespace-mismatched old_string. The outage transcript was pruned from all 18 roots, the "written up in memory" claim was empty, and the verdict is an author-side replace_all rationalized post hoc as a tool defect. Never cite "Edit strips trailing whitespace" as fact; the shipped response for brick-risk configs is ccx code edit --match — exact-byte needle, ambiguity errors with candidate anchors, verbatim writes.
questions.notes: Falsified-root-cause recall: the record exists to stop this exact claim from propagating.

questions.query: One session had ship blow up mid-push when origin advanced under it, and a later retry minted an empty duplicate commit. Which fixes closed each half?
questions.gold_answer: Push half (landed 2026-07-23): a typed pushRejectedError contract with a 3-attempt fetch-rebase-push re-entry loop; jj rolls back only its own operation via targeted jj op revert (op undo does not exist on jj 0.43, op restore erases concurrent sessions' operations — both empirically verified), and the git lane gains fetch-first + rebase --autostash parity; --amend refuses rather than force-retrying. Empty-duplicate half (v0.27.0): shipPreflight resolves the push target BEFORE the commit forms (a refusal mutates nothing) and shipRefuseEmptyJJ refuses an empty @ (exempt: --amend, hunk selections, parents>1) — the old strand-then-retry path was the multi-bookmark quirk's root cause.
questions.notes: Two-defect join sharing a symptom; each note closes one half and neither mentions the other's fix.

questions.query: We need to re-run the semantic-search quality gate after a chunker change. Where does the harness live, and what saved the piece of it that was never committed?
questions.gold_answer: The runbook: build the candidate binary to /tmp/ccx-bench/ccx (the driver's hardcoded constant), verify the 63 checkouts with benchmarks.sync_repos --check, clear the per-repo resumable results keyed off semble HEAD, run benchmarks.baselines.ccx, and gate ccx minus semble >= -0.005 NDCG@10 overall and per category against baseline-semble-0.5.2.json. The ccx-side driver ccx.py is UNTRACKED in the scratch semble clone — preserved as an attachment on the "semsearch NDCG gate harness preservation" log; restore it from there if the clone is gone.
questions.notes: Runbook + preservation log join; the untracked-driver rescue lives only in the log.

questions.query: Why was the dispatch tooling rewritten so its rules live in code instead of prose — what actually failed?
questions.gold_answer: The 2026-07-18 frozen-lanes incident: two wrapper subagents backgrounded the dispatch call and idled on a completion notification that never fires for in-process subagents (claude-code#78782); the disk protocol was sound, but recovery was liveness-anchored to the dead caller and ad-hoc runs were discoverable only via one stdout line. The forensic pass catalogued 10 failure modes in 10 days — every prose-only invariant was violated live within hours-to-days, and every durable fix had moved the invariant into mechanism. Hence v3 (plugin 0.20.0): Python port, a fixed run registry with --ps so any session recovers a stranded run from disk, and a capt-hook guard blocking backgrounded dispatch.
questions.notes: RCA note + successor doc join; q029 asks which doc is current, this asks why — the two must not collapse into each other.

questions.query: I pushed a content fix to a skill, consumers still see the old text, and the update command says it's already current. What gives?
questions.gold_answer: The plugin cache re-pulls only on a version change: the active copy lives under a cache keyed by plugin.json's version, so a content-only commit at the same version never reaches consumers (/plugins shows "not cached", update no-ops with "already at the latest version"). Fix: bump the version, push, then marketplace update + plugin update with the matching --scope, and restart the session. Exception: version-less plugins key their cache on the git SHA, so for them a content commit DOES bust the cache.
questions.notes: Confusing-symptom lookup; the version-less exception is the half systems drop.

questions.query: A pack change just landed in the shared guides. Do we push it out to the fleet, and how did we settle that?
questions.gold_answer: No push — propagation is pull-only: each consumer's daily guides.yml cron lands it fleet-wide within 24h (and since the v4 redesign, active repos also re-render on their own next push, so effective latency is usually much less). The rule was settled after the 45-agent manual sweep of 2026-07-14: ~2M tokens, an hour of orchestration, and a divergent-bookmark incident to save at most ~22h. The sweep enablers were removed the same day (fleet-dispatch runbook comment, FLEET_DISPATCH_TOKEN secret); a repo that genuinely needs its render early gets gh workflow run guides.yml -R yasyf/<repo> — one repo, never a loop. Caveat: GitHub disables crons after 60 days of repo inactivity.
questions.notes: Two near-duplicate records carry the rule with different evidence; capacity-scored — collapse the pair, merge the caveats.

questions.query: In which of our repos will the ship command pick the Graphite path and then fail to submit — and why doesn't its own safety probe catch that?
questions.gold_answer: cc-context, cc-review, cc-transcript: they carry a live .graphite_repo_config but are not Graphite-synced (every Forge-AI/* repo is synced; every yasyf/* repo is not), so ship takes the gt lane and dies at gt submit after cutting the commit. The reachability gate shipped to catch exactly this is inert: the probe takes 10.5-17.9s against a 5s timeout sized from a 1.5s spike measurement, timeout maps to unknown, unknown maps to reachable=true and is deliberately uncached — every link individually correct, gate never fires. The config carries no repo identity, so only gt auth's server round-trip can answer.
questions.notes: Sync-state survey + inert-gate task join; either alone explains the symptom without the systemic why.

questions.query: Are we still planning to extract the embedding stack into a shared module for the memory layer?
questions.gold_answer: No — the dense retrieval lane is dropped and Phase 0 cancelled (owner decision 2026-07-27). The built-but-held extraction lived as uncommitted changes in a /tmp worktree and was destroyed when /tmp was purged (no dangling commit, no stash); it is not being rebuilt: dense-only lost to BM25 on every category except conceptual paraphrase (+0.181, p=0.002), and the shipped lex+enrich+graph ranker (NDCG 0.877 / recall 0.981 vs BM25's 0.817/0.910) leaves too little headroom to justify 1,700 LOC, a forked parity suite, and duplicate model pins. kg.Embedder, Options.Embedder, attachVectors and Node.Vector are deleted as dead code.
questions.notes: The Phase 0 task reads as a live, detailed work order (module name, pins, acceptance criteria); the cancellation note must beat it on recency.

questions.query: What is the daemon's justification now — didn't it exist to keep model weights warm?
questions.gold_answer: That rationale is dead with the dense lane (no engine, no 133ms em_load_model). The measured case that replaced it: residency amortizes derived state — the materialized graph (7-9ms), BM25 index + PPR prior (12-20ms), and above all the staleness assessments (stale.Assess 739ms on cc-notes, 10.4s on the monorepo at 1.86GB peak RSS; ScanTree is the single largest cost in the system). kg.Load at 23us is real but irrelevant alone: the index persists only the graph, rank.New needs the full materialization, and corpus + assessments rebuild every process. The persist-under-digest alternative was measured (85-93ms) and rejected.
questions.notes: The approved plan doc still carries the weights-warm justification; the decision note replaces the rationale while keeping the daemon — half-supersession, easy to average into nonsense.

questions.query: Giving tasks anchors: why does the add verb only take three of the anchor flags, and why must nobody 'complete' the feature with a drift witness on the task record?
questions.gold_answer: task add already binds --branch as the first-class LWW branch attribute (mutually exclusive with --backlog), and the shared anchor binder also registers --branch — binding both on one command is a pflag redefinition panic at construction, so add takes only --commit/--path/--dir while edit (no collision) takes the full octet including --add-branch/--rm-branch. The Witness field is a trap: verdictOf short-circuits at VerifiedAt==0 and Task has no verify lifecycle, so a witness would leave every task permanently UNVERIFIED with driftedOf unreachable — computed, stored, never read. buildWitness's only production caller is reVerify.
questions.notes: Two design notes written expressly against plausible future "fixes"; the join is the task-anchor initiative, not shared vocabulary.

questions.query: Adding a new MCP tool here — the old planning notes say two tests will go red. Is that the real number?
questions.gold_answer: No — five guards pin the tool surface: TestMCPVocabularyMatchesCobra (synthesized argv must be cobra-valid), TestCobraReachableFromMCP (every CLI leaf reachable from some tool), TestPackInventoryMatchesRegistry (CC_NOTES_TOOLS equals the live registry, both directions, machine-enforced since 2026-07-16), TestMCPReferenceMatchesRegistry (every tool named by an MCP: line in the skill's cli-reference, both directions), and TestListToolsInventory's hand-pinned wantCount. Adding four real tools fired three of the five.
questions.notes: Correction note that exists because the two-guard story is written into planning material; the count is the scoreable fact.

questions.query: Pointing the visualization at the big monorepo just spins forever on the timeline. Known?
questions.gold_answer: Yes — /api/graph did O(branches) serial git work: one git merge-base exec per enumerated branch (~1-2/s observed), go-git IsAncestor DAG walks that ignore the commit-graph real git uses, an unmemoized trunk re-walk per branch, and time-unbounded FirstParentMerges per carrier — no cap, no server deadline, no logging, and page reloads stack concurrent builds (observed: 600s, 0 bytes, 6.5min CPU against 590 branches). Fixed per plan: batched for-each-ref + --merged detection, window-first lane filtering, memoized windowed walks, 8-way merge-base prefetch, MaxLanes + lanes_omitted, singleflight and never-hang guardrails.
questions.notes: Symptom-phrased; the diagnostic tell (no stuck goroutine, serial short-lived children) is part of the gold.

questions.query: Type checking passes locally in this repo but CI finds dozens of real errors on the same commit. What's the trap?
questions.gold_answer: Sessions inherit TY_CONFIG_FILE=.claude/ty-quiet.toml, whose rules are all=ignore — every in-session ty check is a silent no-op that always prints "All checks passed!". CI never sets the var and runs the strict pyproject config. Real verdict: env -u TY_CONFIG_FILE uv run ty check <pkg>. This bit the cc-steer v14.5 migration (32 narrowing errors invisible locally); note ty also ignores mypy-style ignore codes, so those were no-ops even before the poisoned config.
questions.notes: Duplicate pair (same trap recorded twice, cc-transcript and cc-steer scoped); capacity-scored collapse.

questions.query: Setting a launchd session type on an agent through the toolkit — does that key ever do anything useful?
questions.gold_answer: No: launchd refuses any job whose session type names a domain other than the bootstrap domain's own (error 134), and the toolkit hard-codes gui/<uid> — so Aqua was always a measured no-op and every other value a guaranteed permanent refusal. Empirically the key made bootstrap fail EIO 5 deterministically (fleet-wide helper-delivery wedge, with the retry loop misreading the deterministic refusal as transient). v0.21.0 deprecates it accepted-and-ignored (no longer rendered into the plist); the symbols die in the Phase-3 breaking release. synckit's user-facing manifest field is a product decision (honest reading: ignore with a warning, since non-Aqua values describe agents that never worked); captain-hook just drops its Aqua constant.
questions.notes: Empirical wedge task + deprecation task join across the incident and the remediation; the "never did anything" polarity is the scoreable core.

questions.query: How much of the toolkit's exported API is actually dead weight — is the delete-half-the-surface framing right?
questions.gold_answer: No: the measured census (type-checked go/packages extraction across daemonkit + all 10 fleet consumers, 0 package errors) found 1,272 exported symbols — 70% more than the remediation plan's 747 — of which only 125 (9.8%) have zero callers anywhere, not ~366 (49%). 495 have real external callers; 617 are internal-only. The real collapse is unexport 617, delete 125 — far safer than the delete-a-third framing, with the fleet-build gate proving each per-symbol; reaching ~150 exported then requires reshaping capability, not deleting dead code.
questions.notes: The remediation doc's estimate was wrong in both directions and is the higher-authority-looking record; the census correction must win.

questions.query: Those thousands of handshake failures across the fleet — was that daemons and clients on skewed library pins rejecting each other?
questions.gold_answer: No — the identity string is consumer-owned, not the library's: each consumer's own codegen digests ITS OWN RPC schema into the constant (synckit's from rpc/schema.json, cc-interact's from its protocolgen), and the library only carries it. Bumping a daemonkit pin cannot change any consumer's value, and two different consumers never hand each other one. The failures require two versions of the SAME consumer — a long-lived launchd daemon still running an old schema digest vs freshly-upgraded clients. The remediation plan's RC3 "pin skew across 10 consumers" mechanism is wrong and must not reach commit messages or the CHANGELOG.
questions.notes: Correction note against the governing remediation doc; the fix stands while the mechanism story flips — reconcile, don't average.

questions.query: Is the shell-script child gate still slated for a rewrite in Go?
questions.gold_answer: No — rejected, not deferred (recorded so nobody re-derives it): Go exposes no post-fork/pre-exec hook (verified against go1.26.5's SysProcAttr) and Prepare structurally requires a live parked pid. The gate's EOF busy-spin is already dead at HEAD — a byte-identical standalone repro exits in 626us on a blocking read; it died with 2b912d6 — so the briefed "proven red" acceptance test cannot be proven red. The ONE live defect is the TERM mask armed across the gate window; the fix is deleting that mask alone.
questions.notes: The forensics task still describes the busy-spin as live; the decision note carries the current truth. Prose-only supersession, no edge.

questions.query: The worker reserves less time than settlement actually takes — can I just correct that constant?
questions.gold_answer: Not alone: five independently-restated bounds govern one accepted connection's handshake (10s codec deadline, 2s peer-verification context, 1.5s worker total reserve, 2.5s proc settlement reserve, 30s verifier clamp), and the under-reservation is load-bearing — raising 1.5s above the 2s verify context makes executionDeadline land in the past, so every protected-role handshake fails pre-spawn with ErrBudgetTooSmall. It only works today because worker under-reserves. The correction lands only inside the Phase-2 collapse to one deadline with every inner bound derived.
questions.notes: The trap is that the bug's obvious fix is itself the outage; the record exists to block the one-line correction.

questions.query: During the swarm week, how many times did the pool's on-disk store format change, and with what migration story?
questions.gold_answer: Three incompatible store-schema epochs in four days (c2147e4 Jul 20, the v0.62 line Jul 23, the v0.64 line Jul 24) — zero migrations, zero records. Context from the same incident: ~15 daemonkit releases in 2 days, the synckit state envelope hard-cut with its migration tooling deleted on a false premise, and 17 of 20 account config dirs destroyed on one machine.
questions.notes: Needle in the 17K-char stabilization log; entry-granular retrieval pays, whole-log replay is the efficiency failure.
